newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/mark probing for new highs in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/mark probing for new highs in late Europe.

text.p: Dollar/mark cruised just beneath its 71-month high in late Europe, and dealers and analysts said further gains were just a matter of time.

German finance minister Theo Waigel gave the mark a brief fillip early on Tuesday when he said Germany wanted a strong currency and the current strength in the dollar and sterling was a market overreaction.

Waigel's words fuelled market fears that a surging dollar might provoke central bank intervention. But those concerns were not enough to prevent the dollar testing above the key psychological level of 1.80 marks.

The dollar was quoted at 1.8006/11 marks at 1520 GMT, off its almost six-year peak of 1.8040 but way up from Monday's late European level of 1.7885/95. It has risen 17 percent since the start of this year, gaining six pfennigs this month alone.
"I think mark weakness will continue -- at the moment I don't see any reason to sell dollars or sterling," said Andy Evenden, senior trader at Bank of Boston here.
Dollar/yen has been overshadowed by the vibrant rallies in dollar/mark and sterling/mark, but it too put on a late spurt, jumping to 115.81/91 from 113.68/73 late yesterday.
Market watchers played down speculation of intervention.
"There is some underlying concern there could be coordinated intervention, but it's not in the interests of anybody at the moment," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
Germany needed a weak mark to boost exports, while the U.S. favoured a strong dollar to help contain inflation and attract overseas investment in its bond market, Stamenkovic said.
Persistent speculation that the single European currency will be broad-based and so weaker than the mark will continue to pressurise the German unit, market watchers said.
U.S. retail sales data out Tuesday undermined the dollar briefly, as the core figure came in lower than expected.

June overall sales rose by 0.5 percent, overshooting average market expectations of a 0.2 increase. A strong auto component, however, meant the gain excluding autos was 0.3 percent -- below the predicted 0.5.
Though the core figure undershot forecasts, analysts said fundamentals remained supportive for dollar/mark.
"Even though the U.S. economy slowed in the second quarter, it's still significantly stronger than the German economy," said DKB's Stamenkovic.
Wednesday sees the release of June CPI data from the U.S., as well as May industrial production and capacity utilisation.
U.S. May business inventories and June real earnings will also appear tomorrow.

Elsewhere, sterling continued to command market attention. The pound hit its highest levels against the mark since October 1990 on Monday, but shed two pfennigs after today's comments from Germany's Waigel.

Sterling/mark later came under renewed pressure when cable tumbled in line with the dollar's fresh advance. The pound was quoted at 3.0173/83 marks and $1.6759/69 at 1604 GMT versus 3.0200/10 and $1.6880/90 in late Europe on Monday.
